scenes.tts: Empty an island of every insect and spider. How many species come back? And are they the same ones? In the Florida Keys, scientists did this to small mangrove islands. Within about two hundred fifty days, most of the islands held about as many species as untreated islands. Yet the species were not all the ones that had been there before.
scenes.caption: Empty an island of every insect and spider. How many species come back? And are they the same ones? In the Florida Keys, scientists did this to small mangrove islands. Within about 250 days, most of the islands held about as many species as untreated islands. Yet the species were not all the ones that had been there before.
scenes.visual: A mangrove island of species dots is emptied; a question mark; the count returns, but some dots are new green ones and some old ones are marked lost.
scenes.narration: Empty an island of every insect and spider. How many species come back? And are they the same ones? In the Florida Keys, scientists did this to small mangrove islands. scenes.tts: A theory published in nineteen sixty three predicted this with two rates. The first is immigration. That means the arrival of a species not already on the island. On an empty island, every arriving species is new. As the island fills, more arrivals belong to species already there. So the immigration rate falls. It reaches zero when every species in the pool is resident. The pool is all the species that could reach the island. Our example uses invented numbers.

scenes.visual: Axes of rate against species on the island; the immigration curve falls from 10 to zero at 100 as a marker fills along the axis.

scenes.tts: The second rate is extinction. Here that means local extinction, the loss of a species from that island. If every resident species has the same, independent chance of disappearing, the extinction rate rises in proportion to the number of species. Draw both curves. They cross at one point. That is the equilibrium. In our example, it is fifty species.
scenes.caption: The second rate is extinction. Here that means local extinction, the loss of a species from that island. If every resident species has the same, independent chance of disappearing, the extinction rate rises in proportion to the number of species. Draw both curves. They cross at one point. That is the equilibrium. In our example, it is 50 species.
scenes.visual: A red extinction line rises from zero; the two curves cross at a yellow point dropped to 50 on the axis.

scenes.tts: The crossing is stable. Above it, extinction beats immigration, and richness falls. Below it, immigration wins, and richness rises. Start with an empty island. The count climbs fast, then levels off. It reaches forty five species, ninety percent of the equilibrium, after about eleven and a half days.
scenes.caption: The crossing is stable. Above it, extinction beats immigration, and richness falls. Below it, immigration wins, and richness rises. Start with an empty island. The count climbs fast, then levels off. It reaches 45 species, 90% of the equilibrium, after about 11.5 days.
scenes.visual: Arrows on the axis push richness toward the crossing from both sides; then a second plot traces richness against days from an empty island.
scenes.narration: The crossing is stable. Above it, extinction beats immigration, and richness falls. Below it, immigration wins, and richness rises. Start with an empty island. The count climbs fast, then levels off. It reaches 45 species, 90% of the equilibrium, after about 11.5 days.

scenes.tts: At the crossing, five species arrive each day. Five species go extinct each day. Net change is zero, so the count holds at fifty. But the species are changing. About five are replaced every day. In the Florida Keys, the second year showed the same pattern. Species numbers changed little, while immigrations and extinctions continued at high rates. The model calls this a dynamic equilibrium.

scenes.tts: A count does not say which species are present. Take a selection of three mite groups from one mangrove island. Before treatment, two were present. A year later, two were present. But only one was on both lists, and three were found in either. To compare lists, divide the species they share by the species found in either list. That is the Jaccard similarity. Here it is one third. A steady count can hide a changing list of species.
